record.paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
record.context_brief: Satellite star formation persistence and rapid quenching
record.original_question: How can satellite galaxies sustain significant star formation for several billion years after being accreted into larger halos and then quench rapidly enough to avoid producing too many galaxies with intermediate specific star formation rates, given that current models with instantaneous or gradual hot-gas stripping still decline too rapidly or fail to match observations?

evidence.quote: active satellite galaxies form stars at a rate that is very similar to that of central galaxies of the same mass, suggesting that the transition from active to passive must be very rapid.
satellite galaxies must have evolved as central galaxies (forming stars at very similar rate) for several Gyrs

It remains unclear how satellite galaxies can sustain significant levels of star formation for several Gyrs, and if this can be achieved by simply relaxing the assumption of instantaneous stripping of the hot gas reservoir associated with galaxies when they are accreted.

artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent literature has converged on a "delayed-then-rapid" satellite quenching paradigm, with starvation (suppression of fresh gas accretion onto the satellite) plus internal feedback emerging as the dominant mechanism, while ram-pressure stripping of the hot halo plays a secondary role, especially at low stellar mass. Observational studies at z~0 and z~0.8 measure quenching timescales of 4–8 Gyr broadly consistent with cold-gas depletion via starvation. Models incorporating these effects reproduce many but not all observed features (e.g. sSFR bimodality and mass dependence are partially matched), so the question is partially solved rather than fully resolved.

status_evidence.title: Star formation and stellar & AGN feedback ... set the quenching timescale in satellite galaxies
status_evidence.snippet: Environmental quenching is driven primarily by starvation in the absence of fresh gas accretion compounded by losses through supernova and AGN feedback, with gas stripping playing a secondary role.
status_evidence.claim: Recent simulations identify starvation plus internal feedback (not hot-gas stripping) as the dominant satellite quenching mechanism.

status_evidence.title: The importance of gas starvation in driving satellite quenching in galaxy groups at z~0.8
status_evidence.snippet: Observed quenching timescales are consistent with satellite quenching via starvation, provided the hot gas envelope of infalling satellites is not stripped away.
status_evidence.claim: Observations at z~0.8 support delayed-then-rapid quenching via starvation rather than instantaneous hot-gas stripping.

status_evidence.title: Both starvation and outflows drive galaxy quenching
status_evidence.snippet: Both starvation and outflows drive galaxy quenching.
status_evidence.claim: Combination of starvation and outflows is needed to explain quenching, supporting partial resolution.
